data.title: Idiopathic guttate hypomelanosis — viva
data.summary: Pigmentary disorders · 5 viva questions with answers
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Idiopathic guttate hypomelanosis** (Pigmentary disorders)_

**Q1. What is idiopathic guttate hypomelanosis (IGH)?**
- Common acquired leucoderma with multiple small (2–5 mm), discrete, porcelain-white, round/angular macules on chronically sun-exposed extensor forearms and shins; increases with age (>40 y), women more; considered a sign of photoageing

**Q2. Pathogenesis.**
- Chronic UV exposure, ageing (somatic mutations of melanocytes), local trauma/friction; HLA-DQ3 association; reduced number of melanocytes and melanin in lesions

**Q3. Histopathology.**
- Basket-weave orthokeratosis, flattened rete, reduced melanin and decreased (not absent) DOPA-positive melanocytes

**Q4. Differential diagnosis.**
- Vitiligo punctata/confetti vitiligo (progressive, Koebner), leprosy (sensory loss), pityriasis versicolor (scale, KOH), post-inflammatory hypopigmentation, progressive macular hypomelanosis (trunk, red follicular fluorescence — Cutibacterium acnes), lichen sclerosus (atrophic), chemical leucoderma, achromic verrucae (flat warts), tinea, guttate morphoea, Darier's (leukoderma)

**Q5. Treatment.**
- Reassurance — benign, cosmetic
- Photoprotection to prevent new lesions
- Options: superficial cryotherapy (2–5 s), focal dermabrasion/needling, fractional CO2/Er:YAG laser, excimer laser 308 nm, topical tacrolimus/retinoids, 88% phenol spot application, 5-FU, mini-punch grafts — variable results

## Quick spotter facts
- Multiple porcelain-white guttate macules on shins/forearms of older adults — IGH

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Acquired hypomelanoses). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
